name: Treaty with the Ottawa, etc., 1807 (Treaty of Detroit)
nations: Ottawa (Odawa) bands of the Maumee, Blanchard's Fork, Auglaize and Roche de Boeuf (Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma)
Saginaw Chippewa (Anishinaabe), including the Swan Creek and Black River bands (Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan)
promises: $10,000 in money, goods, tools or animals after ratification, and a permanent annuity of $2,400 at Detroit divided among the four nations (Article 2).
A reasonable commutation of the annuity if the nations later asked for one (Article 3).
Two blacksmiths for ten years, one with the Chippewa at Saginaw and one with the Ottawa at the Miami (Article 4).
Hunting and fishing on the ceded land so long as it remained the property of the United States (Article 5).
Reserved tracts within the cession for the nations, including six miles square above Roche de Boeuf, four miles square on Miami Bay and three miles square at Macon on the River Raisin (Article 6).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission valued the lands ceded in Royce Area 66 (southeastern Michigan and northwestern Ohio) as of 27 January 1808 at $600,000 for the Ottawa tract, $2,300,000 for the Potawatomi tract and $3,500,000 for the Chippewa tract, found the consideration paid to all three together was $57,717.32, and concluded the consideration was unconscionable.

landTaken: Royce Area 66. The parties agreed the Ottawa tract held 469,116 acres, the Potawatomi tract 1,843,779 acres and the Chippewa tract 3,298,637 acres, 5,611,532 acres in all (Commission opinion of 1978).
compensation: Consideration of $57,717.32 to the three tribes (Commission finding). Net sums set in 1978: Ottawa $579,308.00, Potawatomi $2,292,000.00, Chippewa $3,479,308.00, less offsets. Final awards entered in June 1978 for the Potawatomi and Ottawa.
today: The Commission's title decision (30 Ind. Cl. Comm. 388, 1973) was affirmed by the Court of Claims (207 Ct. Cl. 960, 1975). In that decision the Commission dismissed the Wyandot claim to Royce Area 66 (Docket 140) for want of evidence; that dismissal is a ruling against the Wyandot and is not counted as a breach. The Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma's history says an 1831 treaty required the Ottawa at Blanchard's Fork and Oquanoxie's Village to remove west, and that most Maumee Ottawa were moved in the 1830s.

nationVoice.summary: The tribe's heritage site describes how its Maumee River villages, including Roche de Boeuf and Blanchard's Fork, were expelled from their Ohio homelands and removed to Kansas after an 1831 treaty, with about half of those who left dying within a few years.
